FARRA:v3p251/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p251/r3.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p251/r3.claim: Shafaq is the red glow of the setting sun.

FARRA:v3p251/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p251/r4.speaker: النبي
FARRA:v3p251/r4.claim: A raised report from the Prophet defines shafaq as redness.

FARRA:v3p251/r5.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p251/r5.speaker: بعض الفقهاء
FARRA:v3p251/r5.claim: Some jurists define shafaq as the whiteness remaining after redness vanishes, whose departure marks the night prayer.

FARRA:v3p251/r6.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p251/r6.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p251/r6.claim: An Arab comparison of a garment to shafaq's red color supports the redness interpretation, though he leaves the correct view to God.

TAB-FULL:v24p244/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p244/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p244/r1.claim: The oath pairs the departing day with the arriving night. Al-Ṭabarī prefers shafaq as the day as it recedes; in the legal timing of ʿIshāʾ, shafaq means redness, as he explains in his book on prayer.

TAB-FULL:v24p244/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p244/r2.speaker: بعض أهل العراق
TAB-FULL:v24p244/r2.claim: Some Iraqi scholars define shafaq as the red glow; Mujāhid describes it as redness of the horizon.

TAB-FULL:v24p244/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p244/r3.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v24p244/r3.claim: Mujāhid says shafaq is the whole day, and elsewhere describes it as the redness of the horizon.

TAB-FULL:v24p244/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p244/r4.speaker: بعض أهل التأويل
TAB-FULL:v24p244/r4.claim: Another view treats shafaq as the name for both red and white, making it a word with opposite senses.

ZAJJAJ:v5p305/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p305/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p305/r1.claim: Al-shafaq is the red glow seen in the western horizon after sunset; another view identifies it as daytime.

NAHHAS:v5p185/r23.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p185/r23.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p185/r23.claim: Bā is the basic preposition of oath, with wāw replacing it.

THALABI:v10p160/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p160/r1.speaker: مجاهد وغيره
THALABI:v10p160/r1.claim: They interpret the twilight as the whole daytime.

THALABI:v10p160/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p160/r10.speaker: الخليل
THALABI:v10p160/r10.claim: He says the white twilight does not disappear, recounting that he watched it move from horizon to horizon from Alexandria's lighthouse.

THALABI:v10p160/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p160/r2.speaker: عكرمة
THALABI:v10p160/r2.claim: He interprets twilight as the portion of daylight that remains.

THALABI:v10p160/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p160/r3.speaker: ابن عباس وأكثر الناس
THALABI:v10p160/r3.claim: They identify twilight as the red glow remaining on the horizon after sunset; when it disappears, the first time of the night prayer begins.

THALABI:v10p160/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p160/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود، ابن الزبير، عمر وابنه، عبادة بن الصامت، شداد بن أوس، أنس بن مالك، أبو قتادة، أبو هريرة وجابر بن عبد الله
THALABI:v10p160/r4.claim: These Companions are listed among those who held that twilight is the red glow after sunset.

THALABI:v10p160/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p160/r5.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب، سعيد بن جبير، طاوس، عبد الله بن دينار ومكحول
THALABI:v10p160/r5.claim: These Successors are listed among those who held that twilight is the red glow after sunset.

THALABI:v10p160/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p160/r6.speaker: مالك، الأوزاعي، الشافعي، أبو يوسف، أبو ثور، ابن عبيد، أحمد وإسحاق
THALABI:v10p160/r6.claim: These jurists held that twilight is the red glow after sunset.

THALABI:v10p160/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p160/r7.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز وأبو حنيفة
THALABI:v10p160/r7.claim: They identify twilight as the white glow.

THALABI:v10p160/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p160/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p160/r8.claim: He prefers the red-glow interpretation because the senior authorities agreed on it and Arabic usage and poetry support it.

THALABI:v10p160/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p160/r9.speaker: الفراء
THALABI:v10p160/r9.claim: He cites an Arab description of a bull as red like the shafaq to support the red-glow meaning.

QUSHAYRI:v3p405/r9.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p405/r9.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p405/r9.claim: Shafaq is the redness that follows sunset.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r1.speaker: الكلبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r1.claim: He identifies the twilight as the redness seen in the west.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r2.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r2.claim: He says it is the light remaining on the horizon after sunset and before darkness.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r3.speaker: عكرمة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r3.claim: He interprets the twilight as the remainder of the day.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r4.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r4.claim: He interprets it as the entire day.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r5.speaker: الليث والفراء والزجاج وعمرو عن أبيه
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r5.claim: The language authorities define shafaq as the redness in the sky from sunset until the evening prayer.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r6.claim: The root conveys thinness or delicacy: a thin, flimsy thing is shafaq, and compassion is tenderness of heart.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r7.claim: The red twilight marks the evening prayer time because white twilight lasts longer, while the redness is the sun's remaining light and disappears as it moves farther below the horizon.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r8.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p362#2/r8.claim: An Arab's comparison of a red garment to shafaq provides evidence for the redness interpretation.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:84:6-16/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:84:6-16/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:84:6-16/r5.claim: The negating particle means “I swear”; the twilight is the red after sunset.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:84:6-16/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:84:6-16/r6.speaker: قيل
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:84:6-16/r6.claim: Another view identifies the twilight oath with night and day.

JISHUMI:v10p7342/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7342/r6.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7342/r6.claim: Shafaq originally suggests delicacy or tenderness and means the faint remainder of sunlight after sunset.

JISHUMI:v10p7342/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7342/r7.speaker: الخليل والأوزاعي وأبو يوسف ومحمد والشافعي ومالك
JISHUMI:v10p7342/r7.claim: They define shafaq as the redness of twilight.

JISHUMI:v10p7342/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7342/r8.speaker: أبو حنيفة وثعلب
JISHUMI:v10p7342/r8.claim: They and other jurists and language scholars define shafaq as the whiteness of twilight.

JISHUMI:v10p7342/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7342/r9.speaker: الفراء
JISHUMI:v10p7342/r9.claim: He cites an Arab speaker comparing a red garment to shafaq and lines from poets using the same comparison.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p375/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p375/r3.speaker: مجاهد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p375/r3.claim: Mujahid interprets الشفق as the whole daylight period.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p375/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p375/r4.speaker: عكرمة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p375/r4.claim: Ikrima says it is the remaining daylight.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p375/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p375/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p375/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas and most commentators say it is the redness remaining on the horizon after sunset; others say it is the whiteness following that redness.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p458#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p458#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p458#2/r1.claim: The opening la is extra, yielding an oath; alternatively it rebuts disbelievers before the oath begins.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p458#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p458#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p458#2/r2.claim: God swears by created things to honor them and direct people to take lessons from them.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p458#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p458#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p458#2/r3.claim: Shafaq is usually the redness after sunset, with the accompanying whiteness.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p458#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p458#2/r4.speaker: مجاهد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p458#2/r4.claim: Mujahid identifies shafaq as the whole daytime, a view Ibn Atiyya calls weak.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p458#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p458#2/r5.speaker: أبو هريرة وعمر بن عبد العزيز
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p458#2/r5.claim: Abu Hurayra and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz identify shafaq as the whiteness followed by redness.

TABRISI:84:1-25/r14.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:84:1-25/r14.speaker: مالك والشافعي والأوزاعي وأبو يوسف ومحمد والخليل
TABRISI:84:1-25/r14.claim: They define shafaq as the redness remaining between sunset and the late evening prayer; the Imams also transmit this definition.

TABRISI:84:1-25/r15.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:84:1-25/r15.speaker: ثعلب وأبو حنيفة
TABRISI:84:1-25/r15.claim: Thalab says shafaq is the whiteness of twilight, as does Abu Hanifa.

TABRISI:84:1-25/r16.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:84:1-25/r16.speaker: الفراء
TABRISI:84:1-25/r16.claim: Al-Farra cites an Arab comparison of a red garment to the twilight as evidence for the red meaning.

TABRISI:84:13-19/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:84:13-19/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:84:13-19/r8.claim: Shafaq is the red light remaining on the horizon after sunset; another view says it is the whiteness.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r1.speaker: الحكماء والخليل
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r1.claim: Some philosophers claim whiteness never sets; al-Khalil saw it move from horizon to horizon without disappearing, and Ibn Abi Uways saw it persist until dawn.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r2.speaker: علماؤنا
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r2.claim: They disregard whiteness as the legal boundary because its time is not fixed.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r3.speaker: النعمان بن بشير عن النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r3.claim: Abu Dawud reports the Prophet prayed ʿIshāʾ when the moon set on its third night, giving a defined time; the ruling attaches to the named twilight's onset.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r4.claim: The objection from the first dawn fails because no prayer or fasting rule attaches to it; the Prophet distinguished false dawn by gesture, already explained under fasting in al-Baqara.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r5.speaker: مجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r5.claim: He says shafaq means the whole day, based on the following oath about night gathering what it covers.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r6.speaker: عكرمة
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r6.claim: He identifies shafaq as the remainder of daylight.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r7.claim: Shafaq can also mean inferior or scant things; an ʿaṭāʾ mushfiq is a meager gift, as al-Kumayt's poem illustrates.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16-21/r8.claim: The remaining solar glow and redness is a delicate fading light, matching the root sense of thinness.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r1.claim: The opening particle lā is extra; the sense is an oath.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r2.claim: Shafaq is the redness after sunset, lasting until the time of the late evening prayer.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r3.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r3.claim: Malik and many Companions and jurists identify twilight as the red glow; when it disappears, Maghrib ends and ʿIshāʾ begins.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r4.speaker: الأوزاعي ومالك والشافعي وأبو يوسف وأبو ثور وأبو عبيد وأحمد وإسحاق
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r4.claim: These jurists hold that shafaq is redness.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r5.speaker: ابن عباس وأبو هريرة وعمر بن عبد العزيز والأوزاعي وأبو حنيفة
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r5.claim: An alternative view identifies shafaq as whiteness; Asad ibn ʿAmr reports that Abu Hanifa later withdrew this opinion.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r6.claim: He prefers redness because most early authorities and jurists held it, and Arabic usage, derivation, and Prophetic practice support it.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r7.speaker: الفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r7.claim: An Arab compares red-dyed cloth to shafaq, supporting the meaning of redness.

QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r8.speaker: الصحاح
QURTUBI-FULL:84:16/r8.claim: Shafaq is the remaining light and redness of the sun early in the night, until near darkness.

BAYDAWI-FULL:84:13-19/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:84:13-19/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:84:13-19/r2.claim: الشفق is the redness after sunset; Abū Ḥanīfa says it is the following whiteness, named for its delicacy from شفقة.

QASHANI:84:16-21/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:84:16-21/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:84:16-21/r1.claim: Twilight is the remaining light of human nature after it sets in the body and mixes with ego-darkness; the oath honors its potential for acquired perfection and ascent.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p433/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p433/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p433/r3.claim: Shafaq is the redness after sunset when the time of the final evening prayer arrives; its root is linked to thinness and tenderness.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p433/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p433/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p433/r4.claim: A derivation connects shafaq with something too thin to hold together, and with compassion because the heart softens; a poem uses the word in that sense.

SAMIN-DURR:84:16/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:84:16/r1.speaker: الراغب
SAMIN-DURR:84:16/r1.claim: Al-Raghib defines twilight as daylight mingling with night’s darkness at sunset; ishfaq combines care and fear, with ‘min’ emphasizing fear and ‘‘ala’ emphasizing care.

SAMIN-DURR:84:16/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:84:16/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:84:16/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhshari defines twilight as the redness in the west after sunset; its disappearance ends Maghrib and begins ‘Isha’ for most scholars, while Abu Hanifa reportedly once said it was the whiteness and later recanted according to Asad ibn ‘Amr.

SAMIN-DURR:84:16/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:84:16/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:84:16/r3.claim: There are two twilights, red and white; shafaq and shafaqa are also names for ishfaq, and twilight’s name is linked to delicacy, as is compassion to a tender heart.

SAMIN-DURR:84:16/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:84:16/r4.speaker: الشاعر
SAMIN-DURR:84:16/r4.claim: The poem uses ‘shafaqan’ for fear or tenderness while speaking of loving a life and its death, witnessing the lexical relation to ishfaq.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r1.speaker: علي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r1.claim: Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Abu Hurayrah, and many others identify the twilight as redness.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r2.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r2.claim: A report from Abu Hurayrah defines the twilight as whiteness.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r3.claim: The twilight is the horizon's redness, said by Mujahid to occur before sunrise and conventionally by language scholars after sunset; al-Khalil places it through the evening prayer time.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r4.speaker: الخليل بن أحمد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r4.claim: Al-Khalil defines twilight as the redness from sunset until the time of the late evening prayer, after which it is said to have disappeared.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r5.speaker: الجوهري
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r5.claim: Al-Jawhari describes twilight as the sun's remaining light and redness at the start of night until near deep evening.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r6.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r6.claim: The Prophet says the time for Maghrib lasts until twilight disappears; Ibn Kathir takes this as evidence for al-Jawhari's and al-Khalil's definition.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r7.speaker: مجاهد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r7.claim: Mujahid also interprets twilight in this verse as the whole daytime, and in another report as the sun, because the next oath mentions night.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r8.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r8.speaker: ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r8.claim: Ibn Jarir reads the paired oaths as daytime departing and nighttime arriving.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r9.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r9.speaker: آخرون
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p358/r9.claim: Other authorities say twilight names both redness and whiteness and is therefore a word with opposite senses.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p367#s084/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p367#s084/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p367#s084/r1.claim: Al-Inshiqāq continues the close of al-Muṭaffifīn: allies enjoy reward and enemies receive punishment because they denied resurrection and judgment before their Creator-King.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p372#s084/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p372#s084/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p372#s084/r1.claim: After evidence for resurrection, the oath reassures the denier; leaving an oath over an even clearer claim invites reflection and is more eloquent than swearing explicitly.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p372#s084/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p372#s084/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p372#s084/r2.claim: The shafaq is the western twilight after sunset, passing from red through yellow and murky white to darkness; its name suggests delicacy, as in tenderness of heart.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p372#s084/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p372#s084/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p372#s084/r5.claim: These immense signs and benefits demonstrate God’s complete power to restore things exactly as they were; the resurrection claim is so evident that it needs no supporting oath.

BURSEVI:v10p294/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p294/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p294/r1.claim: Most scholars define shafaq as the red afterglow; when it vanishes, Maghrib ends and the time for Isha begins. Others define it as the white glow that follows, after which Isha begins.

BURSEVI:v10p294/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p294/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p294/r2.claim: The white-twilight view is one report from Abu Hanifa, though he is said to have returned to the majority view; the name suits both meanings because of their delicacy, especially the white light as the Sun’s glow weakens.

BURSEVI:v10p294/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p294/r3.speaker: عكرمة ومجاهد
BURSEVI:v10p294/r3.claim: Ikrima and Mujahid interpret shafaq as daytime, understood as the Sun’s trace, so the oath covers night and day, the periods of rest and work that sustain the world.

BURSEVI:v10p294/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p294/r4.speaker: الراغب
BURSEVI:v10p294/r4.claim: Al-Raghib defines twilight as daylight mixing with the darkness of night at sunset.

BURSEVI:v10p294/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p294/r5.speaker: القاشاني
BURSEVI:v10p294/r5.claim: Al-Qashani reads twilight as the remaining light of human primordial nature after it sets into the body and becomes mixed with the darkness of the self; this light still permits spiritual perfection.

ELMALILI:84:1-21#3/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:84:1-21#3/r16.speaker: author
ELMALILI:84:1-21#3/r16.claim: The opening particle draws the conclusion and affirmation from the preceding exposition.

ELMALILI:84:1-21#3/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:84:1-21#3/r17.speaker: author
ELMALILI:84:1-21#3/r17.claim: Shafaq is the red glow on the horizon after sunset; its root connotes delicacy, as do compassion and fearful concern.

ELMALILI:84:1-21#3/r18.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:84:1-21#3/r18.speaker: author
ELMALILI:84:1-21#3/r18.claim: In Arabic, legal usage, and astronomy, shafaq is the post-sunset red opposite dawn and marks Maghrib; Turkish use for dawn is colloquial.

ELMALILI:84:1-21#3/r19.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:84:1-21#3/r19.speaker: Ebû Hanîfe
ELMALILI:84:1-21#3/r19.claim: Abu Hanifa identifies shafaq as the whiteness that follows the red glow; Abu Hurayra and Umar b. Abd al-Aziz are also reported to hold this view, and Abu Hanifa’s later return to the majority view is transmitted.

ELMALILI:84:1-21#3/r20.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:84:1-21#3/r20.speaker: author
ELMALILI:84:1-21#3/r20.claim: The oath evokes the changing scenes of the world, with each day turning toward evening, first the red twilight and then night and what it gathers.

TABATABAI:84:16-24/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:84:16-24/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:84:16-24/r1.claim: Shafaq is the twilight redness, then yellow, then whiteness that appears in the west early at night.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p238/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p238/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p238/r1.claim: Physical phenomena show gradual change under God's control; humanity too steadily moves toward meeting its Lord, so denying that outcome is foolish.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r1.claim: The opening particle la is discussed in the commentary on al-Qiyamah 75:1.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r10.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r10.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r10.claim: Twilight, night, and the full moon represent changing conditions of light and darkness; their oaths stress human transitions in worldly life and at Resurrection and their cosmic relation.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r15.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r15.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r15.claim: All these changes prove resurrection is possible and that people ought to believe in it.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r2.speaker: Müfessirler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r2.claim: Most commentators define shafaq as the redness visible on the horizon after sunset.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r3.speaker: Mücâhid

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r4.speaker: İkrime
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r4.claim: Ikrima interprets shafaq as the final part of daytime.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r5.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r5.claim: The twilight interval between day and night is brief and hurried, resembling life's short, hurried passage; the oath draws attention to this.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r6.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r6.speaker: Fukahanın çoğunluğu
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r6.claim: Most jurists who define shafaq as redness say the evening prayer time ends when the white twilight appears.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r7.speaker: Ebû Hanîfe ve Evzâî
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:84:16/r7.claim: Those who define shafaq as whiteness hold that the evening prayer time lasts until the horizon darkens.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17#2/r24.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17#2/r24.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17#2/r24.claim: Al-Inshiqāq begins with human toil and successive ordeals, whereas al-Tīn begins by honoring humanity; its fa therefore suits the emphasis on continuing, unclouded reward.

STUDYQURAN:84:16/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:84:16/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:84:16/r1.claim: Al-shafaq is the redness and remaining sunlight after sunset until night, or the interval from sunset until the horizon's last light.
